text: Very early in the morning the chief priests, with the elders and the scribes and the whole council, reached their decision. They bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.

versions.text: Early in the morning the chief priests, with the elders and the scribes and the whole council, reached their decision. They bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.
versions.explanation: The Greek εὐθὺς πρωΐ carries the sense of immediacy ("as soon as it was morning," "very early"), which is lost in the plain "Early in the morning." Adding "Very" preserves the urgency without disturbing the rhythm.

text: Pilate questioned him: "Are you the King of the Jews?" He answered, "You say so."
The chief priests kept bringing many charges against him.
So Pilate questioned him again: "Have you no answer at all? See how many accusations they bring against you."
But Jesus gave no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.

versions.text: But Jesus said nothing more, and Pilate was amazed.
versions.explanation: ἀπεκρίθη is specifically "answered" (responding to the charges), and ὥστε introduces a result clause; "and Pilate was amazed" flattens the cause-and-effect link. "so that" restores the logical connection while keeping the oral flow.

text: Now at the festival he used to release for them one prisoner, whomever they requested.
A man called Barabbas was in prison with the rebels who had committed murder in the uprising.
The crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do what he usually did for them.
Pilate answered them, "Do you want me to release the King of the Jews to you?"
For he knew that the chief priests had handed him over out of envy.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead.
Pilate spoke to them again: "Then what do you want me to do with the one you call the King of the Jews?"
They shouted back, "Crucify him!"
Pilate asked them, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the louder, "Crucify him!"
Wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them; and after having Jesus flogged, he handed him over to be crucified.
The soldiers led him away into the courtyard, that is, the governor's headquarters, and they called together the whole company.
They dressed him in purple, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on him.
Then they began to salute him: "Hail, King of the Jews!"
They struck his head with a reed, spit on him, and knelt down in homage to him.
When they had finished mocking him, they stripped off the purple and put his own clothes back on him. Then they led him out to crucify him.
They forced a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country—the father of Alexander and Rufus—to carry his cross.
They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which means "the Place of the Skull."
They offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he would not take it.
And they crucified him. They divided his clothes among themselves, casting lots to decide what each should take.
It was the third hour when they crucified him.
The inscription of the charge against him read: "The King of the Jews."
With him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.
And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, "He was counted among the lawless."
Those who passed by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads and saying, "Aha! You who would tear down the temple and rebuild it in three days,

versions.text: Those who passed by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads and saying, "So! You who would tear down the temple and rebuild it in three days,
versions.explanation: Οὐά is a jeering interjection of derision; "So!" reads as a mere connective and can be misheard in oral reading. "Aha!" conveys the mocking tone more naturally when read aloud.

text: save yourself and come down from the cross!"
In the same way the chief priests, along with the scribes, mocked him among themselves: "He saved others, but he cannot save himself!
Let the Messiah, the King of Israel, come down from the cross now, so that we may see and believe." Even those crucified with him taunted him.
When the sixth hour came, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.
At the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"—which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
When some of those standing nearby heard it, they said, "Listen, he is calling for Elijah."
Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and held it up for him to drink, saying, "Wait—let's see if Elijah comes to take him down."
But Jesus gave a loud cry and breathed his last.
And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
When the centurion standing there facing him saw how he died, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God."
There were also women watching from a distance. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.
These women had followed him and cared for his needs while he was in Galilee, and many other women had come up with him to Jerusalem.
It was already evening, and since it was the day of Preparation—that is, the day before the Sabbath—
Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who was himself waiting for the kingdom of God, went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
Pilate was surprised that he was already dead, so he summoned the centurion and asked him whether Jesus had died some time ago.
When he learned from the centurion that he had, he granted the body to Joseph.
So Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the linen, and laid him in a tomb cut out of rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
